Why only a short look at metallaboranes?

Structurally they follow the borane pattern: a metal fragment takes the place of a BH vertex. Two slides show this; their chemistry and electron counting belong with the metallaborane notes.

Wade (1971), chs 2–3; Hawthorne (1967), ch. 5; Das, §10.12.

Part A

Diborane: which structure?

Two models, tested by diffraction, infrared and NMR.

A
Part A.
Diborane · the two candidates

Two possible structures for B2H6

Ethane-like · D3d
drag to rotate
  • B–B bond; six equivalent H; C3 axis along B–B.
  • Needs 14 valence electrons; B2H6 has only 12.
Hydrogen-bridged · D2h
drag to rotate
  • No B–B bond; 4 terminal Ht and 2 bridging Hb.
  • Each B–Hb–B bridge is a 3c–2e bond.
Symmetry elements: Wade (1971), Figs 2-1 and 2-2, pp. 7–9 (Wade writes "D2d" for the ethane-like model on p. 7; staggered ethane is D3d). Models: experimental (D2h) and idealised tetrahedral (D3d) coordinates.
Use the buttons to show the symmetry elements. Both models are centrosymmetric, so the zero dipole moment could not decide between them.

Wade (1971), §2-2, pp. 7–14; methylation: H. I. Schlesinger, A. O. Walker, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1935, 57, 621; band counts: H. C. Longuet-Higgins, R. P. Bell, J. Chem. Soc. 1943, 250.
Every row is decided in favour of the bridged structure. The following slides take the three physical methods in turn: diffraction, infrared, NMR.
Diborane · electron diffraction

From a diffraction pattern to bond lengths

Schematic radial distribution curve for the bridged model; dashed lines: Bauer's 1937 maxima.

1. Gas-phase electrons are scattered by every atom pair; the pattern is Fourier-transformed into a radial distribution curve.

2. Each peak is an interatomic distance. Bauer (1937) found 1.32, 1.79, 2.59 Å.

3. The peaks are then fitted to a trial model. Bauer fitted the ethane-like one; Hedberg and Schomaker (1951) fitted the bridged one better.

Why diffraction was slow to decide

H scatters weakly (one electron), so B–Ht (1.19) and B–Hb (1.33) blur into one peak.

S. H. Bauer, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1937, 59, 1096; K. Hedberg, V. Schomaker, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1951, 73, 1482; Wade (1971), pp. 6–7, 13. The 2.57 Å B···Ht distance is calculated from the measured bridged geometry.
The bridged geometry gives B1···Ht(on B2) = 2.57 Å, which explains Bauer's 2.59 Å peak as well as his ethane-like non-bonded B···H did. The lesson: the analysis can only test the trial models put into it.

Distances in pm.

Why X-ray B–H is short

X-rays locate electron density, not nuclei; the one electron of H is pulled towards boron.

Wade (1971), Fig. 2-6, pp. 13–14; Hedberg & Schomaker (1951); W. J. Lafferty, A. G. Maki, T. D. Coyle, J. Mol. Spectrosc. 1970, 33, 345; D. S. Jones, W. N. Lipscomb, Acta Crystallogr. A 1970, 26, 196.
ED and IR agree within 1–2 pm. The B···B distance (177 pm) is close to a single bond length, a sign of B–B bonding through the bridges.
Diborane · infrared

The IR spectrum: click a band to see its vibration

Spectrum redrawn schematically from Wade (1971), Fig. 2-3; frequencies from W. C. Price, J. Chem. Phys. 1948, 16, 894 (ν13, ν17 read from Wade's figure); ν numbers are the standard labels of the 18 normal modes. Displacements qualitative; red arrows show the direction of motion; drag the model to rotate it.
Click any labelled band, or use the buttons. A band appears in the IR only if the vibration makes the dipole moment oscillate; the info line says in which direction. Press A to stop the motion and leave the displacement arrows.
Diborane · infrared

What the IR spectrum proves

  • Four B–H stretches: two near 2600 cm⁻¹ (B–Ht), two at 1600–1850 cm⁻¹ (B–Hb). An ethane-like molecule would give two.
  • Weaker bridge bonds: the B–Hb bands lie ≈ 800 cm⁻¹ lower; one electron pair holds three atoms.
  • Isotope check: in B2D6 the H-dominated bands shift down by ≈ 1/√2.
  • Rotational lines alternate strong, weak: a C2 axis through the borons (Price). A C3 axis would enhance every third line.
Wade (1971), Fig. 2-3, p. 10; Longuet-Higgins & Bell (1943); W. C. Price, J. Chem. Phys. 1947, 15, 614; 1948, 16, 894.
The terminal BH2 modes resemble the CH2 modes of ethylene (Price's comparison); Pitzer described diborane as ethylene with two protons embedded in the π bond. The 1/√2 factor comes from the reduced mass; real ratios are a little higher (about 1/1.35) because B also moves.
Diborane · NMR

NMR counts the neighbours of each H and each B

  • ¹¹B has I = 3/2: H on one B gives a 1:1:1:1 quartet; H on two B gives a 1:2:3:4:3:2:1 septet.
  • Decoupled ¹H: two peaks, 2 : 1 (4 Ht : 2 Hb).
  • ¹¹B: triplet (2 Ht) of triplets (2 Hb); an ethane-like BH3 would give a 1:3:3:1 quartet.
  • J(¹¹B–Ht) ≈ 135 Hz, J(¹¹B–Hb) ≈ 46 Hz: the bridge bonds are weaker.
J. N. Shoolery, Discuss. Faraday Soc. 1955, 19, 215; Wade (1971), pp. 10–13. Stick spectra schematic. (Wade, p. 13, writes 1:2:2:1 for the BH3 quartet; the binomial ratio is 1:3:3:1.)
The 2nI + 1 rule with I = 3/2 gives 4 lines for one boron neighbour and 7 for two.
Diborane · NMR

The recorded spectra

  • Hb is at higher field than Ht.
  • At 100 MHz each Hb line splits into a quintet: weak coupling to all four Ht.
Wade (1971), pp. 10–13, Figs 2-4, 2-5 (reproduced).
Connect the stick spectra with the real traces.

Verdict

B2H6 is the hydrogen-bridged, D2h molecule, with two B–H–B three-centre two-electron bonds.

Wade (1971), §2-2 and Fig. 2-6.

Higher boranes · general

Three kinds of hydrogen, one range of B–B distances

  • H occurs as terminal B–H, in BH2 groups, and in B–H–B bridges.
  • Bridges lie only on the open face of a cage; closo anions have none.
  • The cages are fragments of deltahedra: B5H9 of the octahedron, most others of the icosahedron.
Hawthorne (1967), §5.2, p. 231 (values quoted there in Å); Wade (1971), Figs 3-3 and 3-10.
These numbers recur through the next slides.

Neutron: B–Ht 118 pm; bridge B–H 130 (to B5, 7, 8, 10) and 135 pm (to B6, 9). C2v; styx 4620.

Wade (1971), Fig. 3-10, p. 39 (table reproduced; distances in pm); X-ray: J. S. Kasper, C. M. Lucht, D. Harker, Acta Crystallogr. 1950, 3, 436; neutron: Wade, ref. 7 of ch. 3.
Neutrons are scattered by nuclei, so neutron diffraction locates H properly; the study used 11B- and 2H-enriched decaborane at −160 °C. The bridges are unsymmetrical, slightly nearer B5, 7, 8 and 10.
Higher boranes · ¹¹B NMR

¹¹B NMR: each boron shows how many H it carries

  • B2,4 (BH2, 2 bridges): triplet of triplets.
  • B1,3 (BH): doublet, at higher field.
  • B2,5 (BH2): triplet; B3,4 (BH): doublet.
  • B1: a doublet, not a triplet: its inner H behaves as a near-bridge.
Wade (1971), Figs 3-4 and 3-7, pp. 35–37 (reproduced).
The multiplicity counts terminal H (large J); bridge couplings are smaller and broaden the lines. Integrated areas count the borons.

Carboranes · closo

BH⁻ ≡ CH: the closo carboranes C2Bn−2Hn

1,5-C2B3H5 · trigonal bipyramid
drag to rotate · C grey

BnHn²⁻ → C2Bn−2Hn: same electron count, same deltahedron, no charge.

carboranewhere C sits
1,5-C2B3H5both apices (3-connected)
1,6-C2B4H6trans; more stable than 1,2

Carbon takes low-connectivity vertices, as far apart as possible.

Hawthorne (1967), §5.6B.1–4, pp. 301–302; 2,4-C2B5H7 structure from microwave spectroscopy. Models: idealised deltahedra with C at the observed positions.
1,2-C2B4H6 rearranges to 1,6 at about 250 °C.
Carboranes · icosahedral

C2B10H12: ortho, meta and para

1,2-C2B10H12 · ortho
drag to rotate · C grey

1,2 (450–500 °C) → 1,7 (500–620 °C) → 1,12

  • Ortho C–C: 162.9 pm, shorter than the B–B edges (≈ 177 pm in B12H12²⁻).
  • Para isomer: one ¹¹B doublet, all ten B equivalent (D5d).
  • Heating moves the carbons apart, to the more stable isomers.
Isomerisation: Hawthorne (1967), §5.6B.6a, pp. 302–305; C–C distance: M. G. Davidson et al., Chem. Commun. 1996, as quoted by J. M. Oliva et al., J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2005 (long C–C bonds in carboranes); B–B edge of B12H12²⁻: Wade, Fig. 3-22.
Ortho-carborane is made from B10H12L2 and an alkyne: the alkyne supplies the two CH vertices that close the icosahedron.
Carboranes · nido

Open carboranes: C2B4H8 and the dicarbollide ion

nido = closo minus one vertex

C2B4H8 is B6H10 with two CH for two BH⁻; [C2B9H11]²⁻ is an icosahedron with one vertex missing.

Hawthorne (1967), §5.6B.4 and B.7, pp. 302, 308–310, Figs 5.29, 5.31, 5.32 (reproduced).
The open pentagonal face of dicarbollide is the link to the metallacarboranes in Part D.

Metallaboranes

Fe(CO)3 in place of BH: 1-[Fe(CO)3]B4H8

B5H9
drag to rotate
  • Fe(CO)3 and BH are isolobal: three orbitals, two electrons for the cage.
  • The Fe(CO)3 takes the apex; the B4H8 base keeps its four bridges.
  • Same skeletal count (7 pairs, 5 vertices): nido, like B5H9.
Das, §10.12.11, Fig. 10.12.11.1; model built from B5H9 for teaching (not a measured structure).
CpCo is also isolobal with BH and gives apical and basal isomers.
Metallacarboranes

[Fe(C2B9H11)2]²⁻: the metal completes two icosahedra

[Fe(C2B9H11)2]²⁻ (idealised)
drag to rotate
  • Each dicarbollide binds Fe through its open C2B3 face (η5), as C5H5⁻ does in ferrocene.
  • Fe sits in the missing twelfth vertex of both icosahedra.
  • Fe(II), d⁶, + 2 × 6 = 18 electrons.
M. F. Hawthorne, D. C. Young, P. A. Wegner, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1965, 87, 1818; Hawthorne (1967), §5.7B, Fig. 5.35; Mingos (2021), Fig. 14. Model idealised.
Structure only here; synthesis and electron counting are in the metallaborane notes.
Summary

Key points

  • B2H6 is bridged (D2h): diffraction gives the distances, IR shows two kinds of B–H, NMR counts each H's boron neighbours.
  • In the higher boranes, B–Ht ≈ 119 pm, B–Hb ≈ 133 pm, B–B 170–186 pm; extremes 160 (B6H10) and 201 pm (B10H14).
  • Closo anions are deltahedra with no bridges; nido and arachno boranes are fragments of them.
  • CH replaces BH⁻ in carboranes, and Fe(CO)3 or CpCo replaces BH in metallaboranes, without changing the cage type.
Wade (1971), chs 2–3; Hawthorne (1967), ch. 5; Das, §10.12.
Ask students to sketch B2H6 with all distances from memory.
Check your understanding

Questions (press → to reveal each answer)

1. Why could the dipole moment not decide between the two diborane structures?
Both D3d and D2h have an inversion centre, so both have zero dipole moment.
2. How many ¹¹B NMR lines does an ethane-like B2H6 predict?
A 1:3:3:1 quartet (three equivalent H on each B). Observed: triplet of triplets.
3. Why is neutron diffraction better than X-ray for B–H distances?
Neutrons are scattered by nuclei; X-rays by electrons, which in B–H are shifted towards B.
4. Why is B4–B5 in B6H10 only 160 pm?
It is the one basal edge with no bridging H: a full 2c–2e B–B bond.
Based on these notes.
Allow a minute per question.
